title: Root-sparsity scaling for Hamiltonian simulation, differential equations and linear-system solvers
authors: Dominic W. Berry, Abhishek Rawat, Sophia Simon, Guang Hao Low
abstract: We give quantum algorithms for Hamiltonian simulation, linear differential equations, and linear systems with square-root dependence on sparsity. For an $s$-sparse Hermitian matrix with row and column Euclidean norms bounded by $η$, evolution for time $t$ to error $ε$ uses $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{s}τ+\sqrt{sτ\log(1/ε)}+\log(1/ε))$ queries, where $τ=η|t|$. The same bound holds for time-dependent Hamiltonians with coherent time-indexed sparse access and certified time discretisation. Our construction combines an exact entrywise representation with Cayley transducers. A joint lower bound nearly matches the time, sparsity, and precision dependence, ruling out a uniformly additive bound in $\sqrt{s}τ$ and $\log(1/ε)$. For dissipative linear differential equations we obtain $\mathcal{O}(\bar g[\sqrt{s}(τ+\sqrtτ)+1]\log(C\bar g/ε))$ queries, where $τ$ is the evolution time multiplied by a norm bound, $\bar g$ bounds the ratio of combined input and source norms to the final-solution norm, and $C$ is an absolute constant. We sharpen this bound by separating Hamiltonian and dissipative components, and treat general constant generators. Lower bounds capture joint parameter dependence for time-dependent equations and precision hardness for constant positive semidefinite dissipation. For linear systems, a Cayley walk and Chebyshev filter give $\mathcal{O}(κ\sqrt{s}\log(1/ε))$ queries when $\|A\|\le1$ and $\|A^{-1}\|\leκ$, and we give an alternative proof of a matching joint lower bound. We also give gate-efficient implementations of time-independent Hamiltonian simulation and the dissipative ODE solver, including Lipschitz time dependence, retaining the query bounds with polylogarithmic overhead in inverse precision given efficient entry decoding, arithmetic, and required source preparations.
summary: This paper presents quantum algorithms achieving optimal query complexity for Hamiltonian simulation, solving linear differential equations, and inverting linear systems. The key breakthrough is demonstrating a square-root dependence on matrix sparsity ($s$) for all three problems. These results are significant for quantum simulation theory as they establish tight resource bounds for simulating complex physical dynamics.
main_problem: Developing quantum algorithms to efficiently simulate quantum dynamics, solve linear differential equations, and invert linear systems.
main_result: The authors establish quantum query complexity bounds showing a square-root dependence on sparsity ($\sqrt{s}$) for these tasks, matching established lower bounds.
method: The work employs quantum algorithms leveraging sparse oracle access, utilizing constructions based on Cayley transducers and specialized circuit decompositions.
model_or_system: The algorithms target three distinct computational problems: time evolution governed by a sparse Hermitian Hamiltonian (Hamiltonian simulation), time evolution governed by a general linear ODE (dissipative dynamics), and solving $Ax=b$ (linear systems).
key_observables: Query complexity (number of oracle calls), evolution time ($t$), and required accuracy ($\epsilon$).
important_parameters: Sparsity ($s$), norm bounds ($\eta$), condition number ($\kappa$), and the source/solution norm ratio ($ ar{g}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the sparse-access model, where only non-zero entries of the matrices are accessible via oracles.
figures_summary: TABLE I summarizes the principal matrix-query bounds for Hamiltonian simulation, Dissipative ODE, and Normalised linear system, comparing upper and lower bounds.
paper_structure: The paper systematically derives and compares query complexity bounds for Hamiltonian simulation, dissipative ODEs, and linear systems, establishing optimal scaling with sparsity and precision.
why_interesting: This work provides state-of-the-art theoretical bounds on the resource cost (query complexity) for simulating fundamental physical processes (dynamics and linear algebra) using quantum computation.
